lesson.menu_desc: Most English today has no native speaker in the room -- listening for the gist first, and asking again without sounding rude
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- English Around the World
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 4 -- English Around the World

listenings.text: Hi, it is Lars. Sorry for the voice note, it is faster than writing. So, two things. First, the deadline moved. We now have until the fifteenth, not the eighth, which I think is good news for everybody. Second, and this is the part I want you to think about before Thursday: the client asked whether we can do the whole thing in two phases instead of one. I do not have an opinion yet. I would like to hear yours on the call. That is all. Talk on Thursday.

Hello, this is Bram. I listened to the note from Lars and I want to add one thing before the call. Two phases is possible, but only if we agree now on what goes in phase one. Otherwise everything ends up in phase one and we have solved nothing. I am not against it. I just do not want us to say yes on Thursday and then spend three weeks arguing about the list. So my suggestion is simple: bring your three most important items to the call, and we build the list together in twenty minutes. See you on Thursday.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: To become quieter and stop before finishing the sentence
To keep speaking while the other person is still speaking
To hear something and understand it
To join a conversation with a short comment
To manage to hear or understand something with difficulty
The general meaning, without the details

vocab.text: None of these words is about grammar. They are the words you need to talk about listening itself: what you caught, what you missed, and what you want repeated. In an international meeting, that is half of what you say.

paras: There are roughly four hundred million people who grew up speaking English. There are around one and a half billion who speak it and did not. That second number is the one that matters for your working life, because it means most conversations in English today happen between two people who both learned it.

This has a practical consequence that nobody tells you in a language course. The English you will actually hear is not the English of films. It is a Norwegian speaking carefully, a Dutch colleague going straight to the point, an Indian colleague with a rhythm that puts the stress in a different place. None of them is wrong. All of them are English.

It also changes what good listening means. The native speaker is not the target: understanding is. And understanding does not require catching every word. It requires catching the gist first, and only then going back for detail. Most learners do the opposite. They stop at the first word they miss, lose the thread, and by the time they recover, the speaker has moved on.

The other half of the skill is not listening at all. It is asking. People who work internationally interrupt to check constantly, and nobody thinks less of them for it. The sentence that keeps a meeting on the rails is not a clever one. It is just: sorry, I did not catch that, could you say it again?

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: Why native English is the correct English
Most English has no native speaker in it, so listen for the gist and ask when you miss

items: More people speak English as a second language than as a first.
Roughly four hundred million grew up with it, against around one and a half billion who did not.
The text says non-native accents are a problem to be corrected.
It says none of them is wrong and all of them are English. Understanding is the target, not the native accent.
Good listening means catching every word.
It says understanding does not require catching every word: the gist comes first, detail second.
Most learners stop at the first word they miss.
And by the time they recover, the speaker has moved on — that is how you lose the thread.
Asking somebody to repeat makes you look weak in an international meeting.
The opposite: people who work internationally check constantly, and nobody thinks less of them for it.

items.situation: An American colleague says something you did not hear. You are on friendly terms. Ask again.
tips: Say again? works with Americans and sounds relaxed, not rude.

items.situation: A Norwegian colleague says something you did not catch. Ask again, in a register that fits.
tips: Sorry, I did not catch that. Could you say it again?
Never just What? with a Nordic colleague -- it lands as impatient.

items.situation: You caught the words but not the point. Ask for the gist, not for a repeat.
tips: Sorry, could you give me the short version?
Just to check -- what is the main thing you want from me here?

items.situation: You think you understood, but the decision matters. Confirm before agreeing.
tips: Just to check, are you saying we move the deadline to the fifteenth?
So if I understood you correctly, ...

items.situation: Somebody is talking over you and you have not finished your sentence.
tips: Sorry, may I just finish this point?
Hold on one second, I was not quite done.

items.situation: You lost the thread three sentences ago and the meeting has moved on. Recover without pretending.
tips: Sorry, I lost you at the part about phase one. Could we go back to that?
Naming WHERE you lost it is what makes this work.

answerkey.title: Reveal the whole clarification key
key: Direct, informal (American, Australian): Sorry, what was that? / Say again?
Neutral, works everywhere: Sorry, I did not catch that. / Could you repeat that, please?
Careful (Nordic, formal settings): Sorry, would you mind saying that again?
Asking for the gist, not the words: Could you give me the short version?
Confirming before you agree: Just to check, are you saying ...? / So if I understood correctly, ...
Naming where you lost it: I lost you at the part about ... -- the most useful sentence in this lesson
NEVER: What? on its own with somebody you do not know well. In English it is not neutral.
